pages.text: "Eight waves, nine..." Riri in her yellow hat counted at the windowsill. Outside, the sea was white and wind howled. Dad's motorboat had been tied firmly to the pier post that morning.
"Riri, come away from the window, beside the stove," Mom called. "Just ten! Only ten!" Riri stayed at the sill. Mom added one more piece of wood to the stove.
Then a gust blew—the shutter slammed against the window! Startled, Riri jumped down. "Mom!" She covered both ears.
Mom hugged Riri and took her beside the stove. "It is all right. The wind is rushing past. Farther from the window is safer." Mom's voice slowly calmed Riri's heart.
Mom spread a blanket. Lolo in yellow boots slipped in too. "Shall we pretend we are the soft insides of a clam? This house is our thick shell." Riri felt like a clam inside its shell.

Mom taught three things. "One, move away from windows in strong wind! Two, sit farther inside, beside the stove! Three, come right away when Mom calls!" She tucked the blanket around them. "Strong wind? Beside the stove!"
Though the wind howled outside, all three stayed close under the blanket. Riri held Mom's arm and repeated, "Strong wind? Beside the stove!" This time, she did not count a single wave.
Much later, the wind grew quiet. Outside the open shutters, Lolo splashed those boots in puddles. "Riri stayed so well without crying," Mom said, stroking her head.

Now Riri moved away from the window first whenever the wind grew loud. One, away from windows! Two, farther inside, beside the stove! Three, come when called! Next time, she held Lolo's hand and led the way. Strong wind? Beside the stove!

That evening, Mom hugged both of them in the blanket and rubbed cheeks. However strong the wind, sitting together inside did not feel scary. "Mom, now I will count the three of us in the blanket, not the waves!" Riri said.
